paras: The clubbing of Lem Heard at Heflin depot took place on the night of Sunday, July 31, 1910, when deputies used clubs on a crowd of Black people leaving a district conference at Heflin, Alabama, and knocked Heard, a Black resident of the town, senseless. The only report found, a special dispatch to the Montgomery Advertiser, presented the episode as a near "race riot" that extra police had prevented.

Several thousand Black people had come to Heflin to attend a district conference. On Sunday night many of them were leaving by train, and according to the dispatch they and their friends so crowded the passage to the train that white passengers could not board.

Extra police and deputies were at the depot. The dispatch stated that "it is said" Heard was asked to make room for others and refused, after which "the deputies then began using their clubs." Heard was knocked senseless, and a physician was needed to restore him to consciousness. No other injuries were reported.

By the next day the situation was described as "much more quiet," and no further trouble was expected. No report of arrests, charges, or any inquiry into the deputies' conduct appears in the coverage.

The Montgomery Advertiser ran the Heflin special on August 2 under the headline "Negroes Block Passage of Whites at Heflin." The headline and the opening sentence made the Black crowd the source of the trouble and credited the police with averting a "race riot," while the reason given for Heard's beating rested on unattributed hearsay. The dispatch named no deputy and gave no account from Heard or other Black witnesses. No other white paper and no Black paper was found to have carried the story.

accounts.label: Heflin special dispatch
accounts.gist: A crowd of departing Black conference-goers and their friends blocked white passengers from the train; Heard, said to have refused to make room, was knocked senseless, and deputies then used their clubs; extra police were credited with preventing a race riot.

framing.detail: The headline 'Negroes Block Passage of Whites at Heflin' casts the Black crowd as the problem, and the dispatch credits the police with preventing a 'race riot' while giving Heard's refusal as the reason, on the strength of 'it is said'.
